title: Samsung backs Nvidia AI chip rival in $230 million funding round as GPU alternatives boom
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Key Points:

- Dutch startup Euclyd, which is a building a chip for AI inference that seeks to rival Nvidia, has raised $230 million funding round.
- The round was co-led by Samsung, Somerset Capital Partners, the Scaleup Europe Fund and Innovation Industries.
- A number of tech giants are developing their own AI chips.
Samsung has joined a €200 million ($231 million) funding round for Dutch artificial intelligence chip startup Euclyd, underscoring growing investor appetite for alternatives to Nvidia’s dominant graphics processors.

The Series A round was co-led by Samsung, Somerset Capital Partners, Innovation Industries and the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT. The companies did not disclose Samsung’s individual contribution.

Founded in 2024, Eindhoven-based Euclyd is developing a processor and memory architecture designed specifically for AI inference, the stage when trained models generate answers, images or predictions. Unlike Nvidia’s general-purpose GPUs, Euclyd’s proposed system uses a different architecture that it says can reduce both electricity consumption and the cost of operating AI data centers.

The startup plans to make money in two ways: selling complete hardware racks to enterprises seeking secure, self-hosted AI systems, and licensing its intellectual property to companies that want to develop their own chips. Commercial deployment is targeted for 2028, while Euclyd aims to serve thousands of enterprise customers by 2030.

Samsung’s role could extend well beyond financing. The South Korean technology group is one of the world’s largest memory-chip manufacturers and brings deep expertise in semiconductor engineering, manufacturing supply chains and system design. Euclyd chief executive Bernardo Kastrup said that industrial reach could help the startup move from design to production.

The investment arrives as soaring AI demand strains data-center power supplies and encourages customers to seek cheaper, more efficient processors. Nvidia remains the leader, supported by powerful hardware and its used CUDA software ecosystem. Meanwhile, cloud giants including Google, Amazon and Meta are building custom accelerators, and startups are attacking specialized inference workloads.

Bottom line: Euclyd, however, still faces a long road. Its technology has not been validated in large-scale commercial deployments, and converting ambitious efficiency claims into reliable silicon will require substantial capital, software support and customer trust. (CNBC report summary)
